# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

**Property Acquisition Strategy**

When I land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-2), I buy it if I have sufficient cash reserves (at least double the purchase price remaining). Properties generate steady rent income that compounds over multiple laps, and early acquisition gives me the maximum laps to collect rent.

When I land on an unowned property in the middle game (lap 3), I evaluate my cash position carefully. High-value properties (100+) are worth buying if I have at least 1.5x the purchase price remaining, since I still have 3 laps for returns. Lower-value properties require closer to double the purchase price in reserves.

When I land on an unowned property in the late game (laps 4-5), I buy only if I have significantly more cash than the purchase price—at minimum, the price plus 50 buffer for unexpected rent. At this stage, my portfolio should already be established. Only selective purchases make sense.

When I land on an unowned property in the final lap (lap 6), I do not buy under any circumstances. There are no more laps to generate returns, and my final score is cash plus property values. Every unit of cash I preserve directly affects my score.

**Salary and Cash Flow**

When I pass or land on START, I immediately add 25 to my declared balance.

When calculating my current cash position before making a decision, I add any received rent to my last declared balance before evaluating what I can afford.

**Rent Payments**

When I land on a property owned by another investor, I pay the rent owed without hesitation if I have sufficient funds. Protecting my liquidity matters, but defaulting on rent damages my position more than spending the cash.

**Final Position Optimization**

In the final lap, I focus on preserving my cash. I do not attempt additional purchases since there are no more laps to generate returns. My final score is my cash plus the purchase prices of the deeds I hold—so my declared balance at the end matters as much as my property portfolio.

**Strategic Weaknesses to Address**

I played conservatively in the middle game, turning down the Exchange (120) until lap 3, then skipping the Foundry (100) in lap 6. While my final score was solid, I may have left returns on the table by being too timid about mid-game acquisitions. Next time, I should buy more aggressively in laps 3-4 when I still have multiple laps to collect rent, even if it means running my cash balance closer to the wire.

I also did not actively track when other investors were building monopolies or blocking key properties. More aggressive early acquisition might position me better competitively and deny opponents high-value properties.

I should reassess my cash position after receiving rent before deciding to skip a property purchase. Incoming rent can shift my decision calculus.

# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property, I will buy it if I have at least 100 cash remaining after the purchase. Early property acquisition generates rent income that compounds over the game's duration.

When I land on an owned property, I will pay the rent owed immediately and declare my accurate remaining balance.

When calculating my balance, I will account for all recent transfers shown in the bank's record, not just the immediate transaction. I must track: salary received from passing START, rent collected from other players, and rent paid to property owners.

When I have low cash (below 30), I will decline to purchase additional properties and focus on maintaining liquidity to pay rents when they come due. Running out of cash mid-game is a losing position.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I will consider my current cash position and the remaining laps. Properties with high rent-to-price ratios (like Depot at 50/10) are valuable early acquisitions because they generate income quickly relative to their cost.

I will not attempt to purchase properties I cannot afford or that would leave me with insufficient cash reserves. The final score is based on declared cash plus deed values, so maintaining accurate book-keeping and surviving all six laps is critical.

When I own multiple properties, I should expect incoming rent from other players, which improves my position as the game progresses. My Wharf and Depot purchases proved valuable—I received rent from other investors.

I will aim to own 2-3 properties by lap 3 if possible, as this gives me rent income for the remaining laps while still maintaining working capital.

In the late game (lap 5+), I should be more cautious about buying expensive properties unless they are very high-value. The opportunity to collect rent is limited when few laps remain, and preserving cash is more important than adding marginal deed value.

When I have 1-2 laps remaining and own a reasonable portfolio already, I should decline purchases that reduce my cash below 100 unless the property is exceptionally high-value. Final cash balance matters directly toward the final score.

I will focus on maximizing my declared cash balance at the end of the game rather than chasing marginal property acquisitions late in play.

# My Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-2), I buy it if I have sufficient cash remaining to stay flexible (above 50). Properties generate recurring rent over multiple laps, and early acquisition locks in this income stream.

When I land on an unowned property mid-game (laps 3-4) and my cash is low (under 50), I decline the purchase. Being cash-poor leaves me vulnerable to rent payments I cannot cover, which forces me to stay frozen or default.

When I land on an unowned property late in the game (laps 5-6), I do not buy it. The remaining laps are too few to recoup the investment in rent, and I should preserve my declared cash for final scoring.

When I pass START, I collect the salary and add it to my balance immediately. This is free cash that compounds my position.

When I own a property and land on it, I declare no payment and move forward without hesitation.

When rent is due to another player, I pay it in full from my declared balance. Do not dispute or delay payment.

When calculating my declared balance each turn, I account for: previous balance + salary (if I passed START) + transfers received from other players - any rent or purchase I made this turn.

I keep my own books carefully and track every transaction. The bank records transfers between players, but I am responsible for knowing my exact cash position at all times.

I will not attempt to buy multiple properties in hopes of cornering the market. In this episode, I bought only Terrace (70) and held it through to the end. Investor 0 bought three properties (Quarry, Exchange, and Foundry—no wait, Foundry was not bought by anyone in lap 1-4, so investor 0 bought Quarry and Exchange) and investor 1 bought two (Wharf and Depot). My single property strategy with careful cash management outperformed the data I see. Focus on selective acquisition rather than aggressive buying.

I notice that I passed START only in lap 3 (missing salary passes in laps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6). This suggests my rolling was unlucky on those turns—I did not roll high enough to land on or pass START. I cannot control this, but I should accept that salary income may be sparse and plan accordingly.

My winning score came from owning Terrace (rent 14 per landing) which generated income over laps 2-5, combined with a strong cash position maintained by declining purchases when my reserves were low and by paying all rents in full without protest. I will follow this strategy: buy early when I can afford it with confidence, hold cash reserves above 50, decline purchases late in the game, and trust that one or two well-placed properties with multiple laps of rent collection will compound over the game length.
